extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, mathematics education researchers, teacher educators, and curriculum developers
extracted.subtask_description: A framework for judging when a mathematical argument counts as a proof in school settings: identifies four major features (foundation, modes of argumentation, modes of representation, social acceptance) and related quality criteria, plus functions and common failure modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation (Set of Accepted Statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof rests on statements (axioms, definitions, prior theorems) that are: Known to the audience; Accepted by the audience as true; Made explicit at points where they are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure starting statements are within the conceptual reach of the class and explicitly cited where used; avoid smuggled premises that the audience would not accept. Evaluation asks whether the starting statements are accessible and accepted by the intended community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of Argumentation (Valid Reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument uses valid modes of reasoning such as logical deduction (modus ponens, contrapositive), mathematical induction, case analysis (covering all cases), indirect proof (when used correctly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject empirical generalization from examples as a valid mode for proof. Verify that case analysis indeed covers all cases and that indirect proofs are applied correctly. Computer-assisted or novel methods should still provide deductive validity or be justified to the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of Argument Representation (Form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument is presented using representations the audience can follow: verbal explanation, symbolic algebra, diagrams (when their generality is justified), tables, graphs (when used to indicate, not to prove), and multi-modal combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose representational forms appropriate to the learners' capabilities; justify the generality of diagrams; treat tables/graphs as illustrative unless a general argument is given. Multi-modal presentations can be effective provided each mode's role is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Dimension (Community Acceptance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof's status depends on whether the discourse community accepts the starting points, the rules of inference, the representational choices, and the conclusion as following.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment must consider community norms: what would competent referees/teachers/students accept? Acceptance can vary by audience, so a valid school-level proof may differ from research-level acceptance. Social negotiation and justification may be needed to reach acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Proof (Stylianides)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical argument counts as proof in a community when its foundation, modes of argumentation, and modes of representation are all within the conceptual reach of that community and are accepted by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition as the organising principle: proofs are community- and audience-relative. A proof must satisfy all three pillars (foundation, argumentation, representation) for the relevant community to accept it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of Proof: Conviction and Understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs serve two simultaneous functions: (1) promote conviction — provide grounds to believe the conclusion; (2) promote understanding — explain why the conclusion holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory proof should provide both conviction and understanding. Be wary of arguments that supply only conviction (e.g., black-box appeals to authority) or only understanding (e.g., heuristic explanations that do not establish truth); such proofs are incomplete with respect to the framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied Rubric for Proof Quality (Checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each proof ask: Are the starting statements accessible and accepted? Is the mode of reasoning logically valid (not empirical generalization)? Is the representation appropriate for the audience? Would the community (or a competent referee) accept it? Does it provide conviction that the result is true? Does it provide understanding of why it is true?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to evaluate proofs in teaching and assessment contexts. Each item should be considered explicitly; failing any item indicates a weakness. The checklist operationalises the four features and the two functions into assessable questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-Pattern: Empirical Verification Mistaken for Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Checking many cases (empirical verification) is frequently treated as proof by students and teachers, but this violates the modes-of-argumentation requirement and is not a valid form of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly mark repeated-case checking as a failure mode in rubrics and assessments, even if the conclusion is correct. Teach and assess the distinction between empirical evidence and deductive proof; require general arguments rather than case enumerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting the Framework to Higher/Research Mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The same four features apply to research mathematics with the audience shifted upward: Foundation = prior published results, accepted axioms (e.g., ZFC); Argumentation = must remain deductive (computer-assisted proofs raise questions); Representation = research-level notation, diagrams, computer code as supplementary; Community = referees and readers of the relevant subfield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the framework at higher levels, interpret 'conceptual reach' relative to the research community. Pay attention to issues specific to research practice (e.g., acceptability of computer-assisted proofs, formalisation, reliance on published lemmas) and explicitly justify nonstandard methods to the community.
